extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, study section reviewers, and researchers interested in NIH peer review reliability
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary on how to evaluate the reliability/agreement of NIH grant peer review and on how studies purporting to 'replicate' NIH review should be designed and interpreted. Focuses on sampling, measurement (preliminary vs final scores), reviewer assignment, and what level of variability is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of the range / sample representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The study selected proposals from a very limited range of the applications being reviewed by the NIH (16 already funded by NCI and 9 prior unfunded versions of grants that were funded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valid replication must include a full range of scores/outcomes; restricting to funded or near-funded grants artificially compresses variance and can hide predictive relationships. Conclusions about broad system reliability cannot be drawn from a narrow, non-representative sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate interpretation of correlation in restricted samples
rubrics_metrics.description: The first figure showed little visible correlation of scores, but that can be an artifact of range restriction rather than absence of predictive relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers must understand distributions and correlations: lack of perfect correspondence does not imply lack of predictiveness. Studies should display and analyze the full distribution to avoid misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preliminary (pre-meeting) ratings vs final post-discussion scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper focused on preliminary ratings assigned before the study section meeting rather than final post-discussion priority scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH peer review aggregates multiple reviewers and includes study section discussion that affects final outcomes. Measuring only individual preliminary ratings misrepresents how the system produces final funding decisions and underestimates agreement as realized in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting number of weaknesses is a poor metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors quantified similarities by counting the number of weaknesses listed by reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting weaknesses is meaningless because the impact of a weakness matters (a single fatal flaw can invalidate a grant). Studies should evaluate the substantive impact of strengths/weaknesses rather than raw counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis should reflect multiple reviewers per application
rubrics_metrics.description: The study sometimes compared single reviewers' outputs even though, in the real system, each application is evaluated by more than one reviewer (between two and four in the study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reflect the actual NIH process, analyses should use aggregated reviewer information (e.g., averaged criterion scores or final priority scores) rather than treating single preliminary reviews as the unit of decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and number of panels must be adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used 25 grants and four panels, which commentators regarded as a small sample to draw emphatic conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small n and few panels limit generalizability. Studies about system-wide reliability should include larger, more varied samples to support broad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about generalizability and broad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors stated that their results have 'broad relevance for scientific grant peer review' despite the limited sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must avoid extrapolating from narrowly sampled experiments to the entire NIH system; claims about the whole system require representative sampling and appropriate caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review is inherently subjective; question is expected variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Review by humans is by definition 'subjective'; the important debate is how much variability/precision is acceptable in the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some variation among reviewers is normal. Empirical work should aim to quantify expected precision (e.g., where discrimination is reliable) rather than to assert an unrealistic ideal of perfect agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: System design: reviewers tend to bin applications into tiers, not fine-rank the top group
rubrics_metrics.description: Study section is designed to find the top quarter of grants but often cannot reliably separate within that top tier (e.g., between 10th and 15th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of reliability should focus on the system’s intended function (tiering/binning) and consider whether efforts to finely discriminate within the top group are productive or wasteful; this has implications for setting paylines and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and study section composition affect variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing study sections with reviewers who publish in same journals and share backgrounds produce more consistent evaluations; ad hoc or mixed sections (e.g., ZRGs) produce high variability depending on assigned reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should account for heterogeneity across study sections and the match between reviewer expertise and application topic; reliability estimates should be stratified by section type or reviewer-expertise match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion effects and role of study section meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: The study reportedly did not (or under-) analyze the effect of study section discussion; some evidence suggests discussion can change scores or variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate real-world agreement, include the effect of panel discussion and how it alters preliminary ratings; ignoring discussion misses a key component of the decision process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy relevance: distinguishability near the payline matters
rubrics_metrics.description: If the system cannot reliably tell the difference between, e.g., the 9th percentile (funded) and the 15th percentile (not funded), that's important because funding decisions hinge on such distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies should directly address the system’s capacity to discriminate at policy-relevant cutoffs (paylines) and quantify how much uncertainty exists at those thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency about which reviewer data are used
rubrics_metrics.description: There was confusion/criticism that the paper may have used only primary reviewers’ comments for some analyses while using individual preliminary scores for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must be explicit about which reviewer data (primary vs all reviewers, preliminary vs final) were analyzed and justify that choice relative to the phenomenon being studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical mitigation: use PHS Assignment Request Form to limit variability
rubrics_metrics.description: As a practical step, applicants can use the PHS Assignment Request Form to try to reduce variability by steering assignment to more appropriate study sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not a panacea, assignment requests are a tool applicants should wield to increase the chance of better reviewer-expertise match and lower variability.
